description: AI Village presentations from DEF CON 26 covering machine learning security, AI safety, adversarial techniques, and ethical considerations in artificial intelligence.

talks.title: Identifying and Correlating Anomalies in Internetwide Scan
talks.teaser: Identifying and correlating anomalies in internet-wide network scan data using machine learning.
talks.summary:
Network Scanning Scale

Internet-wide scanning generates massive datasets. Identifying meaningful anomalies in this data is challenging without machine learning approaches.

Anomaly Detection

The presentation covers techniques for identifying anomalies in scan data and correlating them across scans. Understanding patterns in global internet scans reveals infrastructure vulnerabilities.

Machine Learning Application

ML models trained on network scan data can identify unusual patterns, misconfigurations, and potentially vulnerable systems at scale.

Applications

Identifying anomalies in internet-wide scans enables discovery of vulnerable services and infrastructure before attackers do.

He encourages attendees to get involved, submit research, and prepare for an expanded village footprint with new CTF competitions at DEF CON 27.

talks.title: Chatting with Your Programs to Find Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Using natural language interaction with ML to discover vulnerabilities in software programs.
talks.summary:
AI-Assisted Vulnerability Discovery

Natural language processing enables new approaches to vulnerability discovery. Instead of traditional code analysis, conversational interfaces guide the discovery process.

Chatbot Approach

The technique uses chatbots to interact with programs and analyze responses for vulnerability indicators. This approach simplifies complex vulnerability discovery processes.

Program Analysis

Chatting with programs through AI interfaces reveals vulnerabilities through interactive analysis rather than static or dynamic testing alone.

Application

Natural language-driven vulnerability discovery offers new possibilities for security testing and vulnerability identification.

talks.title: Generating Labeled Data From Adversary Sims with MITRE ATT&CK
talks.teaser: Generating labeled datasets from adversary simulations using MITRE ATT&CK framework for ML training.
talks.summary:
Labeled Data Challenge

Machine learning for security requires labeled datasets. Generating realistic labeled data for adversarial scenarios is difficult.

MITRE ATT&CK Integration

Using MITRE ATT&CK framework to simulate adversary behaviors generates labeled data for training ML models. Each simulated attack provides labeled examples.

Adversary Simulation

Running adversary simulations with known attack techniques from MITRE ATT&CK generates training data with accurate labels.

Model Training

Labeled data from adversary simulations enables training ML models to detect attack techniques and adversary behaviors in real environments.

talks.title: Responsible Offensive Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Panel discussion on responsible and ethical approaches to offensive machine learning research.
talks.summary:
Ethical Challenges

Offensive machine learning raises ethical and safety concerns. Researchers must balance innovation with responsibility.

Responsible Disclosure

Finding vulnerabilities in ML systems requires responsible approaches to disclosure and mitigation. Publishing exploits without vendor coordination causes harm.

AI Safety Considerations

Offensive ML research intersects with AI safety. Weaponizing AI requires careful ethical consideration and oversight.

Panel Discussion

The panel covers ethical frameworks for offensive ML, responsible vulnerability disclosure, and balancing innovation with safety in AI security research.

talks.title: The Great Power of AI Algorithmic Mirrors of Society
talks.teaser: Examining how AI systems and algorithms can mirror societal biases and their security implications.
talks.summary:
Algorithmic Bias

AI systems trained on historical data perpetuate and amplify societal biases. These algorithmic mirrors reflect discrimination present in training data.

Second-Order Effects

Bias in AI systems has security and safety implications. Biased ML models in security contexts create exploitable disparities.

Social Impact

AI systems that discriminate against protected groups cause real-world harm. The security community must understand and address these issues.

Mitigation Approaches

Detecting and mitigating bias requires understanding how training data and model architectures perpetuate discrimination. Security researchers must consider fairness in ML systems.

talks.title: Machine Learning Model Hardening For Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Techniques for hardening machine learning models against adversarial attacks and evasion.
talks.summary:
Model Vulnerability

Machine learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that cause misclassification. Hardening models improves robustness against attacks.

Adversarial Training

Training models on adversarial examples improves resistance to attacks. Exposing models to attacks during training builds robustness.

Evasion Resistance

Hardened models resist evasion attempts by adversaries. Techniques include adversarial training, input validation, and defensive distillation.

Practical Hardening

The presentation covers practical methods for hardening ML models in security applications. Model hardening makes systems more resistant to attacks and manipulation.

talks.title: JMPgate Accelerating Reverse Engineering Into Hyperspace
talks.teaser: Evaluating machine learning models for security applications.
talks.summary:
### Vector Space Embeddings for Binary Analysis
At 00:00, Rob and Brandon introduce JMPgate, a machine learning research framework designed to accelerate reverse engineering and binary analysis by mapping compiled assembly code into high-dimensional vector representations.

### Projecting Control Flow into Euclidean Hyperspace
At 07:00, the speakers explain how mathematical vector spaces ("hyperspace") can represent software semantics. Rather than inspecting assembly instructions as disconnected linear text, JMPgate models basic blocks and control flow graphs (CFGs) as semantic embeddings where functionally similar code constructs cluster together in multi-dimensional space.

### Abstracting Instruction Semantics Across Architectures
At 14:04, the researchers tackle the challenge of architecture diversity across x86, x64, and ARM binaries. By training neural models to encode underlying register transformations, memory reads, and arithmetic operations rather than mnemonic string literals, the system achieves architecture-independent representation of assembly logic.

### Overcoming Compiler Optimization Variance
At 21:00, the discussion addresses compiler optimization variances across GCC, Clang, and MSVC. Different optimization levels (-O0 through -O3) drastically restructure basic blocks through loop unrolling, instruction reordering, and register allocation. JMPgate's compositional model learns invariant structural relationships to identify core algorithms despite aggressive compiler mutations.

### Automated Function Identification and Malware Triage
Concluding between 28:01 and 35:01, the authors demonstrate practical reverse engineering workflows. JMPgate rapidly classifies stripped binary functions, pinpoints cryptographic routines, and matches recurring malware subroutines, drastically reducing the manual inspection time required during forensic reverse engineering.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: It is a Beautiful Day in the Malware Neighborhood
talks.teaser: Neural network approaches to cybersecurity challenges.
talks.summary:
### High-Throughput Malware Clustering Challenges
At 00:00, Matt opens his AI Village talk on scalable nearest-neighbor algorithms for malware analysis. He outlines the operational challenge facing threat intelligence teams who must process and classify hundreds of thousands of newly discovered binary samples daily.

### Approximate Nearest Neighbors and Locality Sensitive Hashing
At 05:03, Matt explores the computational limitations of exhaustive pairwise distance comparisons across large binary corpuses. He demonstrates how Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexing and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) reduce quadratic comparison complexity to sub-linear time by hashing similar binaries into shared buckets.

### Building Multi-Index Architectures for Rapid Retrieval
At 10:08, the presentation details the construction of multi-index hashing tables. By partitioning feature spaces across multiple hash tables, analysts can tune the tradeoff between search precision, recall rates, and query latency across millions of samples.

### Feature Extraction from Portable Executable Headers
At 15:30 and 20:58, Matt discusses feature engineering methodologies for Windows Portable Executable (PE) binaries. He details how combining import address tables, section byte-entropies, compiler metadata, and custom similarity hashing creates dense vector representations capable of detecting polymorphic malware families.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Malware Panel
talks.teaser: Threat analysis using defensive AI and machine learning.
talks.summary:
### The Evolving Intersection of Machine Learning and Malware Analysis
At 00:00, moderator Brian Wallace (@BotnetHunter) convenes a panel of leading security researchers, including Dr. Hyrum Anderson (Endgame), to examine the practical realities of deploying machine learning models for malware detection and binary triage.

### Transitioning from Signatures to Structural Feature Vectors
At 05:00 and 10:01, the panelists explore the structural transition from legacy signature detection (such as byte patterns and static YARA rules) to machine learning classification. Modern detection pipelines ingest Portable Executable (PE) headers, import address tables, section entropy, and metadata attributes to recognize malicious software clusters without requiring predefined signatures.

### Adversarial Evasion and Gradient-Based Perturbations
At 15:02, the discussion addresses adversarial machine learning. Panelists examine how threat actors craft adversarial samples by injecting non-functional byte modifications into slack spaces or padding sections, perturbing the feature vector to evade model thresholds while preserving the underlying malicious payload execution.

### Training Realities: Dataset Drift and Ground Truth Contamination
At 20:00, the researchers critique commercial marketing narratives that frame machine learning as an autonomous panacea. They discuss severe operational bottlenecks in production environments, including concept drift as malware evolves, label contamination in public repositories like VirusTotal, and the costly impact of false positives on enterprise security operations centers.

### The Irreplaceable Role of Human Analysts
Concluding at 25:03, the panel reaches a consensus on human-in-the-loop systems. Machine learning functions best as an initial triage filter to process massive sample volumes, but human malware reverse engineers remain essential for interpreting sophisticated evasion techniques, extracting threat intelligence, and validating novel zero-day behaviors.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Adversarial Training
talks.teaser: Techniques and empirical results in adversarial training for hardening neural network models against evasion.
talks.summary:
### Adversarial Attacks Against Computer Vision Systems
At 00:00, Wenqing Cao and Yaohua Guo present their winning competition methodology for generating targeted adversarial images against deep neural networks at the AI Village. They explain how minor input perturbations deceive state-of-the-art vision models.

### Gradient-Based Perturbation Generation
At 02:20, the speakers break down gradient-based attack mechanics, including Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD). By computing gradients of model loss functions with respect to input pixels, attackers craft high-frequency, imperceptible image noise that forces targeted misclassifications.

### Black-Box Attack Transferability Across Architectures
At 04:56, Cao and Guo address black-box attack scenarios where model architectures and weights are hidden from the attacker. They explain how training diverse ensembles of surrogate models generates perturbations that generalize and transfer successfully across unobserved target classifiers.

### Optimization Under Budget Constraints and Submission Limits
At 06:55 and 11:22, the presenters share practical optimization strategies used during competition rounds under strict rate limits. They demonstrate how fine-tuning step sizes and gradient momentum produces robust adversarial samples with minimal query expenditures.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Boosting Adversarial Attacks with Momentum
talks.teaser: Accelerating and stabilizing adversarial perturbation generation using momentum-based gradient optimization.
talks.summary:
### Transferability of Adversarial Attacks on Deep Neural Networks
At 00:00, Xingxing Wei (Tsinghua University) presents research on enhancing the transferability of adversarial perturbations against deep learning computer vision architectures. In black-box threat models where the attacker lacks direct access to model weights and gradients, standard adversarial examples frequently fail to fool target classifiers.

### Limitations of Single-Step and Iterative Gradient Attacks
At 03:00, Wei evaluates conventional attack methodologies. While single-step methods like the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) generate perturbations with reasonable transferability, they lack sufficient attack strength. Conversely, iterative methods like the Basic Iterative Method (BIM) overfit to the specific white-box surrogate model's decision boundaries, resulting in poor evasion rates against unseen black-box defenses.

### The Momentum Iterative Fast Gradient Sign Method (MI-FGSM)
At 06:01 and 09:01, Wei introduces the Momentum Iterative Fast Gradient Sign Method (MI-FGSM). By integrating a momentum velocity term into the iterative gradient update steps, the optimization process memorizes previous gradient directions and smooths the perturbation trajectory, preventing the attack from getting trapped in shallow local extrema.

### Empirical Benchmarks Across Computer Vision Architectures
At 12:01, the speaker presents empirical evaluations across prominent deep convolutional architectures, including ResNet, Inception, and DenseNet. MI-FGSM achieves consistently superior attack success rates in black-box transfers compared to standard iterative attacks, successfully fooling models even when protected by defensive distillation and adversarial training.

### Implications for AI Vision Security and Robustness
Concluding around 15:02, Wei outlines the broader security ramifications for production AI deployments. The high transferability of momentum-boosted attacks demonstrates that deep neural networks share fundamental geometric vulnerabilities in their decision boundaries, emphasizing the urgent need for robust verification and adversarial defense mechanisms.

talks.title: Hardware Trojan Attacks on Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Designing hardware trojan exploits embedded directly into neural network accelerator silicon and hardware.
talks.summary:
### The Threat of Hardware Trojans in Deep Learning Hardware
At 00:00, Joseph Clements presents research on the vulnerabilities of dedicated neural network processing chips at the AI Village. Clements examines how malicious modifications introduced during silicon design or manufacturing compromise deep learning models running on edge devices.

### Embedded Systems Constraints and Specialized Accelerators
At 04:39, Clements reviews the architectural trade-offs of deploying deep neural networks on battery-constrained edge platforms. To achieve real-time performance, mobile systems rely heavily on dedicated ASIC and FPGA hardware accelerators whose complex silicon layouts are difficult to verify.

### Supply Chain Risks in Semiconductor Fabrication
At 09:49 and 14:50, the talk explores semiconductor supply chain vectors. Because modern chip design relies on outsourced third-party fabrication foundries and commercial intellectual property (IP) cores, adversaries can insert dormant hardware trojans into mask sets prior to fabrication without detection.

### Trigger Mechanics and Activation Manipulation in Silicon
At 19:34, Clements details how hardware trojans operate in silicon. By altering arithmetic logic units or modifying internal activation function circuits upon receiving subtle hardware or physical triggers, the trojan forces targeted model misclassifications while behaving normally under diagnostic test suites.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)
